title: History of economic thought
description: Study of the development of economic thought
wiki_lead:
The history of economic thought is the study of the philosophies of the different thinkers and theories in the subjects that later became political economy and economics, from the ancient world to the present day.
This field encompasses many disparate schools of economic thought. Ancient Greek writers such as the philosopher Aristotle examined ideas about the art of wealth acquisition, and questioned whether property is best left in private or public hands. In the Middle Ages, Thomas Aquinas argued that it was a moral obligation of businesses to sell goods at a just price.
In the Western world, economics was not a separate discipline, but part of philosophy until the 18th–19th century Industrial Revolution and the 19th century Great Divergence, which accelerated economic growth.
wiki_excerpt:
The history of economic thought is the study of the philosophies of the different thinkers and theories in the subjects that later became political economy and economics, from the ancient world to the present day.
This field encompasses many disparate schools of economic thought. Ancient Greek writers such as the philosopher Aristotle examined ideas about the art of wealth acquisition, and questioned whether property is best left in private or public hands. In the Middle Ages, Thomas Aquinas argued that it was a moral obligation of businesses to sell goods at a just price.
In the Western world, economics was not a separate discipline, but part of philosophy until the 18th–19th century Industrial Revolution and the 19th century Great Divergence, which accelerated economic growth.


Ancient economic thought (before 500 AD)


Ancient Greece
Hesiod active 750 to 650 BC, a Boeotian who wrote the earliest known work concerning the basic
origins of economic thought, contemporary with Homer. Of the 828 verses in his poem Works and Days, the first 383 centered on the fundamental economic problem of scarce resources for the pursuit of numerous and abundant human ends and desires.


China
Fan Li (also known as Tao Zhu Gong) (born 517 BCE), an adviser to King Goujian of Yue, wrote on economic issues and developed a set of "golden" business rules. Discourses on Salt and Iron in 81 BCE was one of the first recorded debates of state intervention and laissez faire.


Ancient India
The earliest Hindu texts contain no systematic treatment of economics, but they record economic institutions. Joseph Spengler, a historian of economic thought, finds private property, occupational specialization, price-bargaining and interest-bearing loans mentioned in the Rigveda. The later Dharmaśāstras forbid false weights and measures and set the King's tax at between one-tenth and one-sixth of farm produce, and lower for other activities: one day's work for artisans. A customary maximum interest rate was about 1.25% per month. Apart from the Rigveda, other Hindu texts, the Vedas (1700–1100 BC) contain economic ideas, with Atharvaveda (1200 BC) being the most vocal.
In early Buddhist writings, prices are set mostly by custom rather than by the state, and money mediates most trade. The Sigālovāda Sutta advises a householder to divide his wealth into four parts: one to enjoy, two to invest in business, and to save against misfortune.
The most important ancient Indian work on economic policy is the Arthashastra, a treatise on statecraft, military strategy, and the economy traditionally attributed to Chanakya (also known as Kautilya, born ~350 BC) of the Maurya Empire. Chanakya was a minister to Chandragupt Mourya in the fourth century BCE. Its authorship and date are disputed.
The Arthashastra posits that four fields of knowledge are necessary: the Vedas, the Anvikshaki (philosophy of Samkhya, Yoga, and Lokayata), the science of government, and the science of economics (Varta of agriculture, cattle, and trade). All other knowledge, wealth, and human prosperity derive from these four. The text defines the purpose of economics as acquiring what is not possessed, augmenting what is preserved, and bestowing it. Standard histories of economic thought generally begin with the Greeks; some scholars argue that Indian contributions have been largely overlooked.


Greco-Roman world

Ancient Athens, an advanced city-state civilisation and progressive society, developed an embryonic model of democracy.
Xenophon's (c. 430–354 BC) Oeconomicus (c. 360 BC) is a dialogue principally about household management and agriculture.
Plato's dialogue The Republic (c. 380–360 BC) describing an ideal city-state run by philosopher-kings contained references to specialization of labor and to production. grok_lead: The history of economic thought is the study of the evolution of economic ideas across key periods and schools, examining both their logical consistency and their role in guiding human behavior and societal organization, from ancient philosophical inquiries to modern theoretical frameworks. It traces how scholars have analyzed core phenomena such as wealth acquisition, production, distribution, and exchange, influenced by contextual factors like technological change, institutional structures, and methodological shifts. Early origins lie in ancient Greek concepts of oikonomia âhousehold managementâadvanced by Xenophon and Aristotle, who distinguished between natural forms of acquisition like agriculture and unnatural ones like usury, laying groundwork for discussions on value, labor, and justice. These ideas persisted through Hellenistic, Roman, and medieval periods, enriched by Islamic scholars such as Ibn Khaldun, whose Muqaddimah analyzed production, fiscal policies, and economic cycles in societies. The Renaissance and early modern era saw the emergence of mercantilism, which prioritized state power through trade surpluses and bullion accumulation, critiqued for conflating wealth with money rather than productive capacity. The 18th century marked a pivotal shift with the Physiocrats' emphasis on agriculture as the sole source of net product and FranÃ§ois Quesnay's Tableau Ãconomique, followed by Adam Smith's Wealth of Nations (1776), which championed division of labor, free markets, and the "invisible hand" mechanism whereby self-interest promotes social welfare. Classical economics extended these insights through David Ricardo's theory of comparative advantage and rent, and John Stuart Mill's integration of utilitarian principles with distributive justice concerns. The late 19th-century marginal revolution, led by Carl Menger, William Stanley Jevons, and LÃ©on Walras, shifted focus to subjective utility and marginal analysis, resolving debates over value and establishing neoclassical foundations for supply-demand equilibrium. Twentieth-century developments included John Maynard Keynes's advocacy for active fiscal policy to manage demand and avert depressions, contrasting with Austrian School critiques of interventionism by figures like Friedrich Hayek, who emphasized knowledge dispersion and spontaneous order. These schools highlight enduring controversies, such as the merits of market coordination versus government direction, and methodological tensions between deductive theorizing and historical empiricism, with implications for understanding growth, cycles, and policy efficacy. The field's progression reflects causal insights into how incentives, institutions, and innovation drive economic outcomes, informing empirical assessments of prosperity across eras.
